3. On examination, corrected visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally, with normal color vision, visual fields, intraocular pressure, extraocular movements, alignment, and pupils.
4. External examination was notable for left upper eyelid ptosis (Figure 1), with a margin-to-reflex distance 1 of 3.5 mm on the right and 0.5 mm on the left, intact levator function, and no fatiguability on sustained upgaze.
5. There was no evidence of eyelid edema, erythema, or tenderness to palpation.

7. However, Hertel exophthalmometry did not reveal any relative proptosis.
8. No lacrimal gland abnormalities or conjunctival masses were seen with upper eyelid eversion.
9. There was no palpable preauricular or cervical lymphadenopathy.
10. Slitlamp and fundus examination findings were normal.
11. Serological testing results for antiacetylcholine receptor antibody were negative.

4. His ocular history was unremarkable.
5. His uncorrected visual acuity was 20/60 OD and 20/40 OS.

7. Slitlamp examination revealed superficial keratitis and anterior stromal haze in the right eye but otherwise was normal.
8. Fundus examination (Figure, A) revealed a poor foveal light reflex with an irregular-shaped area of red discoloration in the fovea and surrounding subtle flecking of the retina in both eyes.
9. No other abnormalities were found on ophthalmoscopic examination.
10. Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (Figure, B) showed an irregular foveal contour with trace epiretinal membrane formation, with no evidence of foveoschisis or outer retinal changes.
11. Fundus autofluorescence was normal.A, Color fundus photograph demonstrating pseudohole formation with pigment mottling, right eye.
12. B, Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography revealing distortion of foveal contour without epiretinal membrane formation, right eye.
13. Similar examination and optical coherence tomographic findings were present in the left eye.

10. 11. Large choroidal tuberculoma at presentation.
12. In a fundus view of the right eye, a moderate amount of subretinal fluid is seen adjacent to the lesion, involving the fovea center.
13. B-scan (not shown) measured an apical height of 3.4 mm.

6. The mass caused superior displacement of the optic chiasm and had extension into the cavernous sinus bilaterally.  
7. The mass also extended posteriorly and deformed the anterior aspect of the pons (not shown).  
8. After symptom onset, the mass was hyperintense on T2-weighted images (not shown).  
9. During the bedside examination in the postanesthesia care unit, he was noted to have complete bilateral ptosis.  
10. His visual acuity was 20/20 OU with full visual fields on confrontational visual field testing.  
11. He had decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick in the V1/V2 distribution of the trigeminal nerve bilaterally.  
12. The right and left pupils were 5 mm and 6 mm in size, respectively, in both light and dark.  
13. There was no pupillary response to light or accommodation.  
14. No exophthalmos was noted.  
15. Intraocular pressure was normal in both eyes.  
16. The patient was unable to move either eye in any direction on extraocular motility testing.  
17. Vestibulo-ocular reflex did not overcome the ophthalmoplegia.  
18. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was obtained 12 hours after symptom onset redemonstrating the large sellar mass, which no longer had central enhancement (Figure).

1. An Asian woman in her 50s with diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia presented with ptosis and intermittent esotropia of the right eye.  
2. Fourteen years earlier, the patient underwent a pituitary adenoma resection and external beam radiation.  
3. Immediately after the resection, she developed slight ptosis and an adduction deficit of the right eye, presumed to be secondary to partial oculomotor nerve III (CNIII) damage.  
4. Four years earlier, she developed intermittent esotropia of the right eye, presumed secondary to cranial nerve VI palsy.  
5. At the present clinic visit, the patient reported the persistence of intermittent diplopia, which had remained unchanged for years, and denied other ocular or systemic complaints.  
6. Visual acuity measured 20/20 OU.  
7. We noted 3 mm of relative right upper eyelid ptosis and anisocoria (3 mm OD and 4.5 mm OS in ambient lighting).  
8. Pupils were round and reactive with no afferent pupillary defect.  
9. The degree of anisocoria was the same in ambient and dim lighting.  
10. Extraocular movements were initially intact; however, a few minutes later, the patient developed an intermittent esotropia of the right eye, with episodes of sustained adduction lasting up to 30 seconds followed by normalization of ductions and alignment (Video; Figure, A).  
11. These episodes occurred more commonly following voluntary adduction.  
12. On infraduction, the right upper eyelid simultaneously retracted, exposing 3 mm of superior sclera (Figure, B).  
13. On adduction, the right pupil constricted slightly.  
14. The remainder of the examination was within normal limits.  
15. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) from 1 year prior showed a small amount of residual tumor within the right cavernous sinus, stable over years (Figure, C).

3. Since then, he has remained stable with the same dose and schedule of lenalidomide without significant adverse effects.
4. The presenting skin lesions developed 1 month before presentation and began as small pustules that rapidly transformed into painful ulcers.
5. He was treated with valacyclovir for a presumed diagnosis of shingles, but the lesions did not improve.
6. Because of suspected necrotizing fasciitis, he underwent incision and drainage of the lesions.
7. Cultures from the surgical specimen grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus hemolyticus.
8. However, the lesions continued to worsen despite vancomycin and additional debridement.
9. Thus, he was transferred to our facility.

11. 12. Results of additional laboratory studies, including blood culture and tests for herpes zoster virus (via polymerase chain reaction), antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody were all negative.
13. Additionally, the patient also had hypertension and hypercholesterolemia for which he was taking lisinopril and simvastatin, respectively.
14. Pathologic sampling from skin lesions demonstrated a dense dermal infiltrate with predominantly neutrophils along with reactive histiocytes, fibroblasts, and angioplasia (Figure, A).
15. Immunohistochemical staining showed myeloperoxidase-positive neutrophils (Figure, B), histiocytic markers (CD43, CD63, CD168), and CD117-positive mast cells, but no immature myeloid precursors.
16. Results of Grocott-Gomori methenamine silver staining were unremarkable.A, Hematoxylin-eosin staining shows polymorphonuclear neutrophils admixed with scattered histiocytes and vasculatures with a prominent endothelial lining.

13. Anhidrosis was not observed.  
14. Anterior and posterior examination, including of the optic nerve head, had normal results in both eyes.  
15. The cranial nerve, gross motor, and gross sensory examination had otherwise unremarkable results.  
16. The patient’s blood pressure was 160/79 mm Hg.  
17. External photograph demonstrating ptosis of the left upper eyelid.  
18. Magnetic resonance angiography of the brain and neck

1. A woman in her 50s presented to a tertiary dermatology referral center with scaly erythematous patches and plaques covering 10% of her total body surface area without clinically appreciable lymphadenopathy.  
2. Histopathological testing demonstrated an epidermotropic infiltrate of hyperchromatic, convoluted, atypical CD3+, CD4−, and CD8+ lymphocytes with haloed nuclei with basilar tagging and papillary dermal fibrosis.

4. Blood-flow cytometry did not reveal aberrant T-cell immunophenotypes.  
5. She was treated initially with topical and intralesional corticosteroids and narrow band UV B phototherapy.

9. The results of flow cytometry and imaging were unremarkable.  
10. After an initial favorable response with chlorambucil, she developed expanding ulcerated tumors complicated by a polymicrobial superinfection.  
11. Chlorambucil was discontinued in favor of antimicrobial treatment.  
12. She then received liposomal doxorubicin, although skin involvement continued to progress rapidly, with ulcerating tumors making up as much as 80% of her total body surface area.  
13. She was hospitalized for worsening disease and pain (Figure, A).  
14. Repeated histopathologic analysis was done (Figure, B, C, and D).

11. C, Hematoxylin-eosin–stained histologic specimen showing a superficial and deep dermal perivascular and interstitial mononuclear infiltrate with numerous eosinophils (original magnification ×40).

12. Staging imaging revealed bilateral supraclavicular jugular chain, paratracheal and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and the erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 67 mm/h.

Patient_Profile:
1. A 46-year-old healthy Hispanic woman presented with 2 days of photophobia in her right eye.
2. Her best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 20/30 + 2 OD and 20/20 OS.
3. Her intraocular pressure, extraocular motility, and pupillary light reactions were normal.
4. An examination demonstrated trace anterior cells in the right eye; otherwise, the examination had normal results.
5. No vitreous cells were present.
6. Topical prednisolone was started for presumed acute anterior uveitis.
7. One week later, the photophobia had improved.
8. However, unnoticed by the patient, her BCVA had worsened to 20/200 OD and 20/40 OS.
9. An examination demonstrated new subretinal fluid in the macula in the right eye (Figure 1A).
10. Fluorescein angiography showed peripapillary speckled pinpoint areas of hyperfluorescence in the right eye.
11. Indocyanine green showed early choroidal vessel hyperfluorescence and several posterior focal hypofluorescent spots in the midphase in both eyes.
12. Autofluorescence showed patchy hyperautofluorescence in both eyes.
13. Tuberculosis and syphilis testing had negative results.
14. A complete blood cell count was unremarkable.
15. A diagnosis of central serous retinopathy (CSR) was made.
16. The topical prednisolone was stopped.
17. Findings on presentation and follow-up.
18. A, Optical coherence tomography of the right eye demonstrates posterior vitreous cells (white arrowheads), subretinal fluid, and choroidal corrugation (yellow arrowheads).
19. B, Fundus photograph of the right eye demonstrates multifocal, demarcated exudative retinal detachments, including in the macula.
20. Similar findings were present in the left eye.
21. One week later, the BCVA worsened to E at 3 feet OD and 20/200 OS.
22. An examination now revealed 2+ vitreous cells and extensive exudative retinal detachments in both eyes (Figure 1B).
23. No retinal tears were seen on a depressed examination.
24. Retinal detachment repair with vitrectomy and/or scleral buckle

2. She was otherwise well and had no history of tuberculosis or underlying immunocompromise.
3. Her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/80 OD and 20/60 OS.
4. Ophthalmoscopy revealed bilateral swollen, hyperemic optic discs with multifocal yellowish choroidal lesions located at the midperiphery and posterior pole of the retina.
5. The lesions varied in size, ranging from one-fourth to twice the diameter of the optic disc.
6. Punctate areas of choroiditis were also seen along the temporal arcades (Figure 1A).
7. Results of fundus fluorescein angiography showed bilateral early hypofluorescence, with late staining and leakage from the optic discs.
8. Results of systemic examination were normal, except for coarse crepitations of the right lung.
9. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated, at 80 mm/h, as was the C-reactive protein level, at 20.2 mg/L (to convert to nanomoles per liter, multiply by 9.524).
10. Chest radiograph showed consolidation in the right lower zone (Figure 1B).
11. However, results of tuberculin skin test, sputum for acid-fast bacilli, and sputum culture were negative.
12. Three days after initial presentation, the patient developed acute binocular horizontal diplopia and disorientation.
13. A, Color fundus photograph revealed bilateral swollen, hyperemic optic discs with multifocal choroidal lesions.
14. B, Chest radiograph showed consolidation in the right lower zone.

1. An infant boy, born to a nonconsanguineously wed couple, presented to the dermatology outpatient clinic with recurrent skin blisters since age 2 months.  
2. The lesions initially started over the trunk and subsequently progressed to involve the face, hands, and feet.  
3. The episodes of skin blisters were accompanied by pruritus and redness all over the body.  
4. There was no history of oral erosions or difficulty in feeding.  
5. Bowel and bladder movements were normal.  
6. The child had an older sibling who had no skin ailments, and none of the other family members were affected.  
7. On examination, multiple tense, angulated vesicles and bullae on a background of erythema were seen over the face, trunk, and extremities (Figure, A and B).  
8. Few urticated papules and wheals were seen in isolation over the trunk.  
9. The ruptured bullae were healing with hypopigmentation with accompanying scarring and discrete milia formation.  
10. The mucosae and nails were normal.  
11. No contractures or webbing of fingers was noted.  
12. There was no organomegaly.  
13. A punch biopsy from a vesicle was subsequently performed (Figure, C and D).

17. Few urticated papules and plaques can also be appreciated.  
18. C, Subepidermal bulla with bandlike mast cell infiltrate in the upper dermis (hematoxylin and eosin stain).  
19. D, Higher magnification showing dense infiltrate of mast cells in the upper dermis.  
20. Mast cells can be identified by ovoid to spindle-shaped nuclei (hematoxylin and eosin stain).

1. A 65-year-old man was referred for evaluation of uveitis in the left eye.  
2. Several days after YAG capsulotomy for posterior capsule opacification, his left eye had become red and painful and his visual acuity had declined to counting fingers.

8. The results of ophthalmic examination of the left eye were notable for pigmented keratic precipitates, a rare anterior chamber cell, 2+ (ie, 16-25 cells per field) anterior vitreous cells, epiretinal membrane, and cystoid macular edema.  
9. Tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, syphilis, and HLA-B27 laboratory test results were negative.  
10. The macular edema improved with 4 times daily topical prednisolone acetate and ketorolac tromethamine.  
11. After 2 months, the patient reported recurrent pain, redness, and decreased visual acuity.  
12. At that time, the visual acuity in the left eye was 20/200E at 2 ft, and there were 4+ (ie, >50 cells per field) anterior chamber cells, a layered hypopyon and 2+ anterior vitreous cells.  
13. A subsequent vitreous tap and injection of intravitreal vancomycin hydrochloride (1.0 mg) and ceftazidime (2.25 mg) were performed.  
14. Cultures yielded 1+ Propionibacterium acnes.

11. Total bilirubin level was 23.9 mg/dL; aspartate aminotransferase, 252 U/L; and alanine aminotransferase, 100 U/L.
12. Venous lactate level was 49.6 mg/dL.
13. A computed tomography scan of the head was unremarkable.
14. A thin preparation blood smear was obtained (Figure).

1. A 66-year-old woman with chronic hepatitis B infection and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) presented with subacute epigastric pain.
2. Three years prior, she was diagnosed with a solitary HCC and underwent surgical resection with curative intent.
3. Pathology revealed poorly differentiated HCC, 16 cm in largest dimension, with large vein involvement (T3bNXM0, R0 resection).
4. The patient underwent expectant observation.
5. One and a half years prior to the current presentation, laboratory results revealed an elevated α-fetoprotein (AFP), and cross-sectional imaging revealed multiple lung nodules consistent with metastases.
6. She was treated with nivolumab every other week and attained a biochemical (baseline, 212.2 ng/dL; best response, 3.3 ng/dL) and radiographic complete response.In the current presentation, the patient reported nonradiating epigastric pain of moderate intensity for 1 month.
7. Associated symptoms included nausea, anorexia, and water brash without emesis.
8. Review of systems was positive for unchanged chronic abdominal bloating and negative for other constitutional or gastrointestinal symptoms.
9. Laboratory results, including liver function tests, amylase, lipase, and AFP, were within normal limits, and hepatitis B virus polymerase chain reaction was undetectable.
10. Computed tomography with multiphasic liver protocol showed new enlarged mesenteric nodes and diffuse thickening of the gastric body (Figure, A).
11. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) identified diffuse inflammation and ulcerations in the gastric body and antrum (Figure, B).
12. Biopsy specimens showed chronic and active mixed inflammatory infiltrate, including intraepithelial lymphocytosis (Figure, C).
13. No overt viral cytopathic effects were observed, and immunostaining results for Helicobacter pylori, cytomegalovirus, and adenovirus were negative.A, Coronal view of restaging computed tomography of chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast.
14. The yellow circle notes borderline enlarged mesenteric nodes inferior to the stomach, and the yellow arrowheads show thickened gastric body wall.
15. B, Gross appearance of the gastric mucosa visualized via upper endoscopy, which showed diffuse inflammation and ulceration in the gastric body and antrum.
16. C, Biopsy of the gastric mucosa showed marked chronic and active intraepithelial infiltration of lymphocytes (blue arrowheads) and neutrophils (yellow arrowhead) and associated glandular epithelial injury with withered glands and gland dropout (red circle) (original magnification ×100).

1. A woman in her mid-30s pregnant with twins at 13 weeks’ gestation presented with a tender right-flank mass, which she noticed after falling and sustaining trauma to the area 1 week previously.
2. Medical history was significant for a total thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid cancer 7 years before as well as a strong family history of malignant breast cancer on the maternal side and colon and liver cancer on the paternal side.
3. Physical examination revealed an 8 × 8-cm, tender, firm posterior right-flank mass that was mobile but fixed to the abdominal wall musculature.
4. Laboratory examination revealed no abnormalities.
5. Ultrasonography demonstrated a hypoechoic lesion measuring 3.3 × 3.6 cm with internal echoes and no significant flow (Figure 1A).
6. A noncontrast magnetic resonance image (MRI) revealed this to be a well-circumscribed T2 hyperintense lesion with diffuse surrounding soft tissue edema within the adjacent muscular and subcutaneous tissues abutting the posterior margin of the right chest wall and external oblique muscle at the level of the T11 to T12 intercostal space (Figure 1B and C).
7. A, Ultrasonography demonstrating a hypoechoic mass in the musculature of the right flank.
8. B and C, T1- and T2-weighted images demonstrating an enhancing right-flank mass within the right-flank musculature.
9. Because of the concern of malignancy, an ultrasonography-guided core biopsy was performed and demonstrated a myofibroblastic proliferation with immunostains positive for actin and negative for S100 and desmin.
10. Her case was presented at the soft tissue tumor board, and given that the patient was asymptomatic and pregnant, the decision was made to closely watch the progression of this lesion with serial imaging with a planned resection after delivery.
11. Unfortunately, she developed premature rupture of membranes and lost the pregnancy.
12. Follow-up computed tomography was not able to identify the lesion but MRI showed that it was still present but decreased in size (2.4 × 1 cm) with interval resolution of surrounding inflammatory changes.
13. She subsequently underwent wide local resection of the lesion.

1. A young man in his late teens presented with numerous atrophic papules and plaques on his trunk and extremities that developed gradually over several years.
2. Although most were asymptomatic, the patient was concerned about the ongoing appearance of new lesions and the associated pain that some lesions were causing.
3. His medical history was significant for adenosine deaminase–deficient severe combined immunodeficiency (ADA-SCID), which had been managed since childhood with twice weekly intramuscular injections of pegademase bovine enzyme replacement, thrice weekly trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis prophylaxis, and monthly infusions of intravenous immunoglobulin.
4. Physical examination revealed 9 smooth-surfaced, skin-colored to hyperpigmented, 0.5- to 1.5-cm atrophic papules and plaques that exhibited the buttonhole sign on palpation (Figure, A).
5. The multicentric lesions were located on the left knee, left thigh, bilateral chest, and back.
6. Punch biopsies of lesions on his trunk and extremities were sent for histopathological examination with hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) staining (Figure, B and C), immunohistochemical (IHC) studies, and molecular evaluation with reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction.A, The patient presented with 2 distinct, smooth-surfaced, 0.5- to 1.0-cm atrophic plaques with overlying hyperpigmentation on the left thigh.
7. Both lesions exhibited the buttonhole sign on palpation.
8. B and C, Histopathology shows poorly circumscribed hypercellular proliferation of spindle cells occupying the lower reticular dermis with lacelike infiltration of the subcutaneous fat (hematoxylin-eosin).
9. The somewhat whorled, uniform appearing spindle cells with mildly hyperchromatic, elongated, wavy nuclei surrounded by pale cytoplasm.
10. Mitotic figures and nuclear pleomorphism are uncommon.

1. A 5-year-old girl was referred to a pediatric gastroenterology clinic for chronic constipation and poor weight gain.  
2. During her first week of life, she developed diarrhea and vomiting.  
3. With initiation of solid food, she developed laxative-dependent constipation.  
4. She underwent newborn genetic screening before routine cystic fibrosis (CF) screening.  
5. Results were normal.  
6. At the time of presentation to the gastroenterology clinic, she had no respiratory symptoms.  
7. Results of anorectal manometry, spinal magnetic resonance imaging, and thyroid studies were normal.  
8. Family history included constipation in a sister and a great aunt with CF.  
9. Her body mass index (BMI) was below the third percentile (eFigureA in the Supplement).  
10. Physical examination findings were unremarkable, including normal respiratory examination.  
11. Fecal elastase level was within reference range (>500 μg/g); abdominal computed tomographic image revealed a dilated, tortuous sigmoid colon; and full-thickness rectal biopsy was negative for Hirschsprung disease.  
12. She was referred for sweat chloride testing to assess for CF.  
13. Results of 3 separate sweat chloride tests were indeterminate (Table), prompting pulmonology referral.  
14. A 97-mutation CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) analysis panel was negative.  
15. Whole-genome sequence analysis revealed 1 CF-causing mutation (c.2249C>T) and 2 likely benign variants (c.1408A>G and c.2562T>G).  
16. No further testing; the patient does not have CF

A woman in her 50s with a history of nasal-type natural killer (NK)/T-cell lymphoma (diagnosed 2 years prior; treated with pembrolizumab and methotrexate, ifosfamide, etoposide, dexamethasone, and pegaspargase) and chronic pulmonary coccidiomycosis being treated with fluconazole was admitted for fever, hypotension, and rash.
2. Three months prior, pembrolizumab treatment was stopped because of a widespread morbilliform reaction, which had resolved completely 6 to 8 weeks before admission.
3. The new widespread, asymptomatic skin eruption had been ongoing for 1 to 2 weeks and appeared different from her pembrolizumab reaction.
4. A complete blood cell count was notable for a normal white blood cell count of 4100/μL, normal absolute neutrophil count of 2940/μL, chronic normocytic anemia (hemoglobin level of 8.2 g/dL), and chronic thrombocytopenia (platelet count of 62 ×103/μL).
5. Blood culture results showed no growth at 1 week.
6. Serum β-D-glucan, galactomannan, Coccidioides antibody by complement fixation, and immunodiffusion results were negative.
7. Respiratory viral panel and SARS-CoV-2 test results were negative.
8. Total body skin examination findings were notable for widespread, nontender, erythematous patches and thin plaques, some with prominent overlying telangiectases and hyperpigmentation (Figure, A).
9. A punch biopsy of a representative lesion was performed (Figure, B-D).
10. A, Physical examination findings were notable for widespread erythematous patches and thin plaques, some with prominent overlying telangiectases.
11. B and C, Hematoxylin-eosin stained section.
12. D, CD56 immunostaining labels intravascular atypical cells.

Patient_Profile:
1. A girl in her teens presented with a unilateral itchy nodule on her right labium majus of 4 months’ duration.
2. The patient was born and lived in a rural village in Malawi.
3. Her medical and family history were unremarkable.
4. She did not report fever or malaise.
5. Physical examination revealed a polypoid, rubbery tumor measuring 1.5 cm located on her right labium majus, which obliterated the right labium minus (Figure, A).
6. She did not present with enlarged lymph nodes, and results of the physical examination were otherwise unremarkable.
7. An incisional lesional biopsy was taken (Figure, B and C).
8. A, Polypoid nodule on the right labium majus obliterating the labium minus.
9. B-D, Hematoxylin-eosin–stained lesional specimens.
10. B, Histopathologic analysis of the nodule showed pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia with transepidermal elimination of basophilic oval-shaped structures in the epidermis and a dense acute and chronic dermal infiltrate in the dermis.
11. C, Numerous dermal structures surrounded by a dense acute and chronic inflammatory cell infiltrate with granuloma formation.
12. D, High-power magnification of the oval parasitic structures with a typical terminal spine.

Haptoglobin: 10 mg/dL (Normal: 41-165 mg/dL)  
Indirect bilirubin: 2.7 mg/dL  
D-dimer: <250 ng/mL (Normal: <250 ng/mL)  

A peripheral blood smear shows reticulocytosis and microspherocytes.

10. Cerebrospinal fluid studies were remarkable only for an elevated white blood cell count of 72/μL (79% lymphocytes) and elevated protein level at 97 mg/L, while Gram stain and culture were negative.

9. Patient_Profile:
1. A woman in her 60s with a history of bilateral proliferative diabetic retinopathy complicated by a recent vitreous hemorrhage in her left eye presented with an acute onset of redness, irritation, and blurred vision in her left eye.
2. Her symptoms started 1 day after she rubbed her left eye with her hands after handling the milky latex (a fluid found in 10% of flowering plants) of a plant in her garden.
3. She had no recent history of recent eye surgery, eye trauma, cold sores, or new illnesses.
4. On presentation, her visual acuity was 20/40 OD and 20/200 OS.
5. Her pupils were equal, round, and reactive in both eyes.
6. Her intraocular pressures were 16 mm Hg OD and 19 mm Hg OS.
7. On anterior segment examination, she was found to have pinpoint epithelial defects, thickened stroma, and dense Descemet folds, along with a nuclear sclerotic cataract (Figure 1).
8. Central pachymetry in the left eye measured 706 μm, which was elevated from the mean expected pachymetry values of 540 to 560 μm.
9. A posterior pole examination was limited by corneal edema, but there was evidence of a vitreous hemorrhage.
10. The fellow eye had no corneal edema and was pseudophakic, with prior panretinal photocoagulation scars in the peripheral retina.

7. Results of cardiopulmonary, abdominal, neurologic, and dermatologic examinations were unremarkable.
8. Results of laboratory testing, including complete blood cell count, basic metabolic panel, and liver function tests, were within normal limits, and results for HLA-B27 were negative.

12. Plain radiographs of the hands and pelvis at presentation.

5. Bilateral dorsiflexion weakness was present (4 of 5).  
6. There were otherwise no motor deficits, muscle atrophy, or lateralizing neurologic abnormalities.  
7. On arrival, the patient underwent a stroke/transient ischemic attack workup.  
8. Results of a comprehensive metabolic panel, complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, and a coagulation panel were within normal limits.  
9. Computed tomography angiogram demonstrated no evidence of extra or intracranial dissection.  
10. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain with and without contrast (Figure) demonstrated symmetric, bilateral, restricted diffusion, with T2 hyperintensities in the supratentorial white matter and corpus callosum.  
11. Lumbar puncture was obtained and revealed normal cell counts and no oligoclonal bands or evidence of infection.  
12. A, Diffusion-weighted imaging sequence demonstrating bilateral, symmetric, restricted diffusion of the supratentorial white matter (corresponding hypointensity noted on apparent diffusion coefficient sequences).  
13. B, T2 sequence demonstrating bilateral and symmetric increased signal in the supratenorial white matter–sparing U-fibers.  
14. The patient had reportedly always walked on the outside of his feet and had been considered clumsy when compared with other children but had no history of motor delays.  
15. Family history revealed a mother with diminished reflexes, hand tremor, and balance issues with a prior inconclusive electromyogram and nerve conduction study.  
16. A younger brother with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder also had similar gait abnormalities.

Patient_Profile:
1. A man in his late 60s with a diagnosis of type 2 diabetes for more than 10 years that was complicated by neuropathy and retinopathy presented with persistent chorea in the left upper extremity for about 1 month despite aggressive correction with insulin.
2. He was alert and oriented with healthy vital signs.
3. No evidence of cognitive impairments was present on bedside testing results.
4. The patient denied any recent infections and risk for human immunodefiency virus (HIV) infection.
5. Neurological examination results were significant for choreiform and hemiballistic movements involving the left upper extremity.
6. His home medications were carefully reviewed to rule out any medications that could cause chorea.
7. A review of his previous records indicated an admission to an outside facility 3 weeks beforehand with severe hyperglycemia and a hemoglobin A1c level of 14.1% (to convert to the proportion of total hemoglobin, multiply by 0.01).
8. Despite an aggressive correction of blood glucose levels and metabolic correction, his choreiform movements had remained unresolved.
9. On admission, a complete electrolyte and toxicology panel, including calcium, magnesium, and phosphorus, yielded normal results.
10. The patient’s serum glucose level was 159 mg/dL (to convert to millimoles per liter, multiply by 0.0555) and his hemoglobin A1c was 10.9% without ketoacidosis.
11. Test results for antinuclear antibodies, lupus anticoagulants, and antiphospholipid antibodies were negative.
12. Serum thyrotropin levels, liver function test results, and parathyroid hormone levels were healthy.
13. Copper studies, a peripheral smear, and a routine electroencephalogram yielded normal results.
14. A general screening for cancers yielded negative results.
15. The patient underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) (Figure), which showed a T1 hyperintensity in the right caudate head and a lentiform nucleus with no restricted diffusion.
16. Oral administration of olanzapine, 2.5 mg daily, in divided doses with careful monitoring of blood glucose levels resulted in the complete resolution of chorea.
17. Magnetic resonance imaging shows T1 hyperintensity in the right caudate head (A) and a lentiform nucleus with no restricted diffusion (B).

1. A 33-year-old woman with a history of hereditary bilateral retinoblastoma as an infant presented to a primary care clinic with 1 week of right lower extremity swelling.
2. At age 8 months, she was treated with right enucleation and left eye radiotherapy (50.4 Gy).
3. At age 4 years, she developed a recurrence of the retinoblastoma in the nasal cavity and was treated with 4 cycles of vincristine, doxorubicin, and cyclophosphamide followed by 1 cycle of cisplatin, etoposide, and intrathecal cytarabine.
4. Primary care evaluation was prompted by her mother, as the patient had not noticed her lower extremity edema.
5. She had no fevers, weight loss, shortness of breath, chest pain, abdominal pain, or history of deep vein thrombosis.
6. Her physical examination was notable for firm, nonpitting edema to the hip.
7. She did not have any associated tenderness, inguinal lymphadenopathy, or palpable abdominal masses.
8. Her vital signs were within normal limits and she ambulated comfortably.
9. Laboratory work results, including a complete blood cell count with a differential, comprehensive metabolic panel, and D-dimer levels, were within normal limits.
10. Doppler ultrasonography of her right lower extremity showed no deep vein thrombosis.
11. A computed tomography venogram demonstrated a 4.0 × 3.5 cm mass of likely vascular origin that was extending into the right common iliac vein (Figure).

11. Cranial nerve examination was otherwise unremarkable.  
12. Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed no remarkable abnormalities except for partially empty sella (Figure 1B).  
13. She had normal blood pressure levels.  
14. Results of laboratory testing regarding systemic infection were negative, and her serum D-dimer level was normal.

Patient_Profile:
1. A 32-year-old Nigerian woman presented with dull pain, pruritus, and discoloration of the dorsal aspect of both feet for 18 months.
2. Her medical history included a red blood cell transfusion as a child and 2 uncomplicated pregnancies.
3. The lesions started as small papules on the dorsal right great toe and left third toe that gradually spread across the dorsum of her feet over the following 12 months.
4. An over-the-counter antifungal ointment was unhelpful.
5. Her primary care physician completed a biopsy, diagnosed verruca plantaris, and prescribed topical salicylic acid twice daily for 4 weeks.
6. The lesions did not improve, and her foot pain worsened.
7. Subsequent treatment with topical liquid nitrogen cryotherapy was ineffective.
8. Three months after cryotherapy, the patient presented to the dermatology clinic regarding the lesions on her feet.
9. The patient stated that the lesions had been stable in size for the previous 6 months, without bleeding, discharge, or change in color.
10. She continued to have 6 of 10, dull, constant pain that was nonradiating, improved when she soaked her feet in water, and worsened with any type of topical pressure or wrapping.
11. Physical examination revealed multiple well-circumscribed, scaly plaques with cobblestone surfaces on the dorsal aspects of the forefoot and midfoot bilaterally.
12. Findings were more severe on the right and left hindfoot (Figure, left panel).
13. On serologic testing, the patient was negative for HIV and positive for hepatitis C virus (HCV).
14. A punch biopsy of the right foot lesion revealed psoriasiform epidermal hyperplasia, parakeratosis, eosinophils, papillary dermal inflammation, and intraepidermal necrosis (Figure, right panel).
15. Left, Dorsal aspects of bilateral forefoot and midfoot of a 32-year-old Nigerian woman.
16. Right, Punch biopsy of the patient’s right foot lesion (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×40).

Patient_Profile:
1. A young man presented for a second opinion regarding acquired color blindness and visual loss.  
2. He was recently hospitalized for confusion, short-term memory loss, vomiting, and diarrhea.  
3. He also experienced hair loss (Figure 1), a facial rash, hoarseness, and painful peripheral neuropathy in his feet.  
4. His blood pressure on admission was 150/102 mm Hg, his pulse was 118 beats/min, and ophthalmic examination findings demonstrated decreased visual acuity and dyschromatopsia.  
5. He reported difficulty opening his eyelids during hospitalization but denied any history of diplopia.  
6. Results of a complete blood cell count, comprehensive metabolic panel, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were within reference limits, and computed tomography of the head without contrast showed no abnormalities.  
7. A lumbar puncture showed normal opening pressure with a mildly elevated protein level in the cerebrospinal fluid.  
8. Alopecia was noted in our patient in addition to temporal thinning of the lateral half of the eyebrows.  
9. On our examination, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/70 OU.  
10. Extraocular motility was full in both eyes, and confrontational visual field test findings were full in all quadrants.  
11. The patient missed 4 color plates on Ishihara pseudoisochromatic testing.  
12. The slitlamp examination revealed an unremarkable anterior segment, and results of dilated ophthalmoscopy showed temporal optic nerve pallor in both eyes.  
13. The macula, vessels, and retinal periphery were unremarkable on examination.  
14. Automated perimetry showed bilateral central scotomas, and results of a multifocal electroretinogram were normal.

2. The lesions had started about 6 months previously as recurrent crops of pruritic erythematous papules that subsided leaving behind brownish-bluish black hyperpigmentation after each episode.
3. On examination, there were multiple, brown, hyperpigmented patches symmetrically affecting her neck, axillae, antecubital fossa, and intermammary and inframammary areas (Figure, A).
4. The patches showed a reticulate pattern at the peripheries.
5. Intermammary patches had central erythema and a few subsiding papules.
6. Additionally, there were dark brown to bluish-gray patches with reticulation on the lower back and dorsum of the neck (Figure, B).
7. These patches also had a few resolving erythematous papules in the periphery.
8. There was no history suggestive of allergic rhinitis or bronchial asthma.
9. Her IgE levels and thyroid status were normal.
10. Her fasting blood glucose and basal insulin levels were not raised.
11. There was no family history of similar lesions.
12. The rest of the skin, nails, and mucosae were all normal.
13. Potassium hydroxide mount analysis from skin scrapings did not reveal fungal hyphae or spores.
14. A skin biopsy was performed from lesions on the lower back, and the specimen was submitted for histopathologic analysis (Figure, C and D).
15. A, Illustrated are multiple brown hyperpigmented patches symmetrically affecting the neck, axillae, antecubital fossa, and intermammary and inframammary areas.
16. The patches show a reticulate pattern at the peripheries.
17. The intermammary patches have central erythema and a few overlying edematous papules.
18. B, Bluish-gray pigmented patches with prominent reticulation on lower back.

Patient_Profile:
1. A 70-year old man with a history of soft contact lens wear presented for a general eye examination.
2. Visual acuity was 20/20 OU with normal intraocular pressure.
3. Several giant follicles were noted on the right inferior palpebral conjunctiva, and a few smaller follicles were noted in the left inferior fornix.
4. Papillae were also noted bilaterally on the superior palpebral conjunctiva.
5. He did not report any redness or discharge but did note mildly increased irritation mainly from soft contact lens wear.
6. He had endorsed proper contact lens care and hygiene.
7. He also noted an upper respiratory tract illness 4 weeks before presentation.
8. Initially, he received a giant papillary conjunctivitis diagnosis because of soft contact lens intolerance and a recommendation to take a contact lens break.
9. Because of the papillary reaction, prednisolone acetate, 1%, twice a day for 2 weeks was prescribed.
10. After 3 months, the symptoms had improved in the left eye, but conjunctival follicles were still present in the right inferior palpebral conjunctiva (Figure 1).
11. The patient subsequently underwent testing for chlamydia and gonorrhea, and the result was negative.
12. At the 1-year follow-up, the examination findings were unchanged.
13. During this follow-up, Lyme disease and Epstein-Barr virus serologic tests were performed in addition to repeated chlamydia testing.
14. The results were negative, except for a positive Epstein-Barr virus IgG.
15. Slitlamp photograph showing prominent large follicles (arrowhead) in the right inferior palpebral conjunctiva.

Patient_Profile:
1. A woman in her late 50s was referred to the neuro-ophthalmology clinic for evaluation of a 7-month history of recurrent, transient vision loss in the right eye.
2. She reported 5 episodes, each lasting a few minutes and all occurring on awakening.
3. Further inquiry revealed that symptoms always developed after using her electronic reader tablet in dim lighting while lying on her left side.
4. Notably, the patient reported immediate resolution of vision loss on turning on the lights.
5. She denied headaches, visual aura, or neurologic symptoms.
6. Her other medical history was unremarkable.
7. Six months prior to presentation, workup at her local hospital for the transient vision loss revealed an enhancing right orbital mass on magnetic resonance imaging (Figure, A).
8. Carotid ultrasonography and head magnetic resonance angiography showed no abnormalities.
9. Inflammatory marker levels were normal.
10. Magnetic resonance imaging 3 months later showed a stable mass without change in size or appearance.
11. A, T1-weighted magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the orbit with contrast shows a well-circumscribed, enhancing soft-tissue lesion in the right orbit superomedially (arrowhead).
12. B, Computed tomographic (CT) scan of the orbit with contrast shows the mass (arrowhead); no change noted on Valsalva maneuver.
13. On examination, visual acuity was 20/25 OD.
14. Pupils, intraocular pressure, and motility were unremarkable.
15. Anterior segment examination showed mild cataract and dry eye.
16. Posterior pole examination revealed evidence of posterior vitreous detachment and normal optic nerves with 0.2 cup-to-disc ratio in each eye.
17. The retina was flat without evidence of whitening or Hollenhorst plaques.
18. Humphrey visual fields were full.
19. Normal retinal nerve fiber and ganglion cell layer thickness were observed in each eye on optical coherence tomography.
20. Computed tomography of the head revealed no change in orbital lesion size with Valsalva maneuver (Figure, B).

1. A 3-year-old girl with no medical history presented to the emergency department with 1 day of abnormal gait and bilateral mydriasis.  
2. Two weeks prior, she had upper respiratory symptoms and bacterial conjunctivitis treated with topical ofloxacin.  
3. On examination, pupils were fixed and dilated to 8 mm, extraocular movements were intact, and fundus examination was normal.  
4. She had brisk reflexes, poor coordination, and a wide-based unsteady gait.  
5. Bloodwork revealed leukocytosis and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate; cultures remained without growth.  
6. Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid studies, computed tomography scan, and magnetic resonance imaging of brain and orbits were normal.  
7. The patient was discharged 3 days later following improvement in lethargy and gait with a diagnosis of acute cerebellar ataxia.  
8. When she presented to ophthalmology for 1-week follow-up, her visual acuity was central, steady, and maintained in both eyes.  
9. She demonstrated sluggish but reactive pupils and new-onset ophthalmoplegia.  
10. She was unable to move either eye in any direction, including with doll’s head maneuver.  
11. She was readmitted to the hospital and demonstrated diminished reflexes bilaterally and unsteady gait.  
12. Repeat magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated diffuse enhancement of the lower thoracic and cauda equina nerve roots and enhancement of the left oculomotor nerve (Figure).  
13. Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine (A) showing diffuse enhancement of the lower thoracic and equina nerve roots and of the brain (B) showing asymmetric enhancement of the left oculomotor nerve (arrowhead).

10. Examination by an otolaryngologist revealed normal tympanic membranes and a dry but otherwise normal nasal mucosa on flexible endoscopy.  
11. 12. Kidney function was within normal limits.  
13. Chest radiograph results were unremarkable.  
14. False-color and red-free (inset) fundus photograph of the right eye shows retinal pallor (white arrowheads) with a cherry red spot (yellow arrowhead) in the macula (A).  
15. Optical coherence tomography of the right macula shows hyperreflectivity and thickening of the inner retinal layers (yellow arrowheads) and hyporeflectivity of the outer retinal layers (blue arrowheads), except for increased signal intensity in the outer retinal layers of the fovea (white arrowhead) (B).

1. A 69-year-old man with a history of relapsed acute myeloid leukemia (AML) monocytic type presented with intermittent fever and fatigue 2 months after allogeneic stem cell transplantation (SCT).
2. Post-SCT bone marrow biopsy specimen analysis at day 30 showed no evidence of leukemic cells and 99.5% donor cells.
3. His home medications included acyclovir, fluconazole, and cyclosporine.
4. Temperature on admission was 103.1° F, and other vital signs were unremarkable.
5. Vancomycin and cefepime were started for possible infection.
6. Complete blood cell counts with differential counts showed no evidence of peripheral blasts.
7. Laboratory and imaging work-up—including chest radiographs, blood culture, fungal culture, urinalysis, sputum culture, respiratory viral panel, fungitell and galactomannan assay, coccidioidomycosis serology, and cytomegalovirus and human herpesvirus 6 polymerase chain reaction assays—were all negative.
8. The patient was discharged with oral antibiotics after being afebrile for 72 hours.
9. Thereafter, he had 2 more emergency department visits and was readmitted for recurrent fever.
10. A thorough physical examination revealed 2 nonpruritic skin bumps on the right forearm and left calf that both measured 1.0 cm × 1.5 cm.
11. Both bumps were soft without pigmentation or ulceration.
12. Pathologic sampling of the respective lesions revealed a diffuse infiltration of large mononuclear cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio (Figure, A and B).
13. Immunohistochemistry staining was positive for CD4 cells and myeloperoxidase (Figure, C and D)A and B, Histologic evaluation of the skin biopsy specimens.
14. C and D, Immunohistochemical analysis.

5. On examination, there was left cervical and inguinal lymphadenopathy and no other organomegaly.
6. Complete blood cell count and peripheral blood smear showed marked leukocytosis, with a white blood cell count of 22 340/μL, an absolute neutrophil count of 5360/μL, and 55% eosinophils with an absolute eosinophil count of 12 290/μL (to convert all to cells ×109/L, multiply by 0.001).
7. Vitamin B12 was markedly elevated at more than 4000 pg/mL (to convert to pmol/L, multiply by 0.7378).
8. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 5 mm/h.
9. Lactate dehydrogenase was 180 U/L, and alkaline phosphatase was 81 U/L (to convert both to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167).
10. Evaluations for HIV and hepatitis B and C were all negative.
11. Serum creatinine was 0.76 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 88.4); alanine aminotransferase and aspartate aminotransferase were 11 U/L and 9.9 U/L, respectively (to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167); and total bilirubin was 0.35 mg/dL (to convert to μmol/L, multiply by 17.104).
12. Bone marrow biopsy showed hypercellular marrow (cellularity of 100%), myeloid hyperplasia, increased eosinophils with some dysplasia, and a blast count of 2%.
13. Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic scan showed a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm and a left inguinal lymph node of 3.1 × 2.3 cm with an standardized uptake value max of 5.7 (Figure, A).
14. Left inguinal lymph node biopsy showed partial involvement by atypical cells with high proliferation index (Ki-67 >95%) that were positive for CD3, CD4, CD8, BCL2, and TDT, suggestive of T-cell lymphoblastic lymphoma/leukemia (Figure, B).A, Positron emission tomographic–computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan of the head and neck at presentation showing a left upper cervical lymph node of 2.6 cm (arrowhead).
15. B, Lymph node biopsy immunohistochemical stain with terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase.
16. The inset shows interphase fluorescence in situ hybridization for FIP1L1::PDGFRA rearrangement (positive).
17. C, PET/CT 12 weeks after treatment initiation.Myeloid/lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia and tyrosine kinase gene fusions

3. The onset was simultaneous in both eyes, with no associated eye pain or photophobia.
4. There was no ocular history, and a recent comprehensive eye examination had normal results.
5. Her visual acuity was 20/20 OU.

7. There was no vitritis, and her optic nerves were pink and sharp.

9. These spots were hyperautofluorescent on fundus autofluorescence and localized to the subretinal space (Figure 1).
10. 14. No lymphadenopathy or other skin lesions were noted.

15. Vital signs and results from complete blood cell count and thyroid function tests were normal.
16. Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging, angiography, and venography of the brain and orbits revealed extraocular muscle enlargement and enhancement and a dilated superior ophthalmic vein OD.

11. Hemoglobin level was 10.6 g/dL (reference range, 13-17 g/dL); calcium, 8.1 mg/dL (reference range, 8.5-10.1 mg/dL); potassium, 6.2 mmol/L (reference range, 3.5-4.7 mmol/L); and phosphorous 8.8 mg/dL (2.8 mmol/L) (reference range, 2.5-4.9 mg/dL [0.81-1.58 mmol/L]).

13. Urinalysis showed minimal albuminuria (100 mg/dL); however, spot urine protein to creatinine ratio predicted 11 139 mg/g (reference range, 0-200 mg/g) proteinuria.
14. Renal ultrasound showed no hydronephrosis.
15. Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation electrophoresis identified a small monoclonal IgG κ band.
16. Serum κ free light chain (FLC) level was 20 765 mg/L (reference range, 3.3-19.4 mg/L) with a free κ to λ ratio of 296 (reference range, 0.37-3.1).1 Hemodialysis was initiated and a bone marrow biopsy obtained.
17. Bone marrow biopsy showed a normocellular bone marrow with 10% κ-restricted plasma cells (Figure, left panel).
18. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity for the plasma cell marker CD138 (Figure, right panel).

Patient_Profile:
1. A 55-year-old white woman presented with 1 week of decreased visual acuity and ache on abduction in the right eye.
2. She had decreased right-sided hearing and tinnitus, a moderate right-sided frontal headache, and an unsteady gait.
3. She did not have diplopia, facial numbness, or paresthesias.
4. She had a history of stage IV breast cancer treated with letrozole after a mastectomy 5 years prior.
5. On an initial examination, her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/50 OD and 20/25 OS, with dyschromatopsia, relative afferent pupillary defect, and visual-field defects on the right side.
6. Her extraocular movements were full.
7. A dilated fundus examination demonstrated a pale right optic nerve.
8. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain was reported to have normal results, but on review, we noted thickening and enhancement of both optic nerves (with the right eye larger than the left eye), cranial nerve III in the right eye, cranial nerve V bilaterally, the pituitary infundibulum, and the hypothalamus, as well as adjacent cavernous sinuses.
9. Leptomeningeal thickening over the convexities of the anterior frontal lobes was also evident.
10. The patient’s cerebrospinal fluid contained a small population of polyclonal CD19+ B cells and CD4+ and CD8+ T cells.
11. An extensive laboratory workup, including tests for HIV, antinuclear antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, serum protein electrophoresis, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, complete blood cell count, antiganglioside antibodies, anti–myelin-associated glycoprotein antibodies, and angiotensin-converting enzyme, gave normal results.
12. A computed tomographic (CT) scan of the thorax and a whole-body positron emission tomography (PET)/CT scan revealed no abnormalities.
13. Clinically, she initially responded to corticosteroids.
14. Over the ensuing 5 years, she had multiple similar presentations that also included facial pain and paresthesias.
15. She also developed a chronic small-fiber peripheral neuropathy and was treated with mycophenolate mofetil, cyclophosphamide, and intravenous immunoglobulin at various points.
16. She remained clinically stable for 4 years and returned with similar symptoms.

Patient_Profile:
1. A 4-year-old girl with newly diagnosed acute lymphocytic leukemia, receiving her initial course of chemotherapy with vincristine, daunorubicin, and methotrexate, developed a painful lesion on her left triceps.
2. The tender area was beneath an adhesive bandage placed where she had received DTaP (diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis) and polio vaccinations 3 weeks earlier.
3. Otherwise, she appeared remarkably well, and her vital signs were normal.
4. Removing the bandage revealed a tender indurated gray-violet plaque (Figure, A).
5. White blood cell and neutrophil counts were low at 0.4 K/μL (normal range, 4.86-13.18 K/μL) and 0.18 K/μL (normal range, 1.60-8.29 K/μL), respectively.
6. Blood culture findings were negative.
7. Punch biopsy specimens were obtained for histopathologic analysis (Figure, B) and fungal culture (Figure, C).
8. A, Gray-violet plaque on posterior upper arm at site of adhesive portion of bandage.
9. B, Broad nonseptate hyphae surrounding and infiltrating dermal blood vessels (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×400).
10. Of note, occasional septae are seen in this specimen, consistent with the characteristic finding that mucormycetes are pauciseptate, rather than aseptate, molds.
11. C, Nonseptate hyphae with round terminal sporangia and free spores (lactophenol cotton blue mount; original magnification ×400).

Patient_Profile:
1. A woman in her 60s was diagnosed with high-grade leiomyosarcoma of the uterus in 2017 for which she underwent total abdominal hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy.
2. In 2020, she relapsed in the liver and spine.
3. In November 2020, she underwent posterior lateral stabilization of C7-T4 for a T2 vertebral body metastasis causing cord compression, followed by postoperative stereotactic body radiation therapy to T2 to T3 (35 Gy/5 fractions) in January 2021.
4. In February 2021, she received palliative radiation therapy (20 Gy/5 fractions) to T9 to T12 for a T11 vertebral body metastasis with epidural extension.
5. From January to August 2021, she was treated with gemcitabine, and in September 2021, she received her first dose of liposomal doxorubicin.
6. Two weeks later, she developed progressive bilateral lower extremity numbness, pain, weakness, and imbalance, prompting emergent evaluation.
7. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings demonstrated extensive spinal cord edema extending from T2 to the conus and a posterior ring-enhancing intramedullary lesion at T9 to T10 without any mass effect (Figure 1).
8. Because the intramedullary lesion appeared atypical for malignant disease given the lack of mass effect, she was prescribed high-dose steroids while further workup was pursued.
9. Lumbar puncture showed no malignant cells.
10. Positron emission tomographic-computed tomographic (PET/CT) scan demonstrated multifocal intensely F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid disease, but only mild uptake from T9 to T12 and no definitive FDG-avidity at the intramedullary lesion.
11. Her symptoms remained stable with steroid treatment and a plan was made to repeat an MRI of the spine in 6 to 8 weeks.A, T1-weighted postgadolinium sagittal image demonstrating an enhancing spinal intramedullary lesion (blue arrowhead).
12. Of note, there was enhancement of the previously irradiated T11 vertebral body metastasis, and adjacent vertebrae demonstrated marrow hyperintensity on T1-weighed noncontrast imaging.
13. B, T2-weighted short τ inversion recovery imaging demonstrating extensive spinal cord edema (blue bracket).Spinal cord infarct: underlying cause workup, supportive care

1. A 50-year-old woman presented to the emergency department for 3 months of right orbital pain.
2. Her medical history was noncontributory.
3. Examination revealed a right afferent pupillary defect, visual acuity of hand motion OD and 20/30 OS, full extraocular movements, and bilateral retinal dot blot hemorrhages.

7. A, Contrast enhancement centered on the right intracanalicular optic nerve (blue arrowhead), involving right orbital apex and posterior ethmoidal sinus (white arrowhead).
8. B, Enhancement encircling right optic nerve (arrowhead).Orbital apex and sinus biopsy revealed acute and chronic inflammation without neoplasm or microorganisms.
9. Specimen cultures grew methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA).
10. The patient was diagnosed as having type 2 diabetes and MSSA sino-orbital infection.
11. She was discharged 10 days later with intravenous (IV) antibacterials, sitagliptin, insulin, and oral opiates.The patient returned to the emergency department 2 weeks later with recurrent orbital pain.

14. Pain rapidly resolved, repeated MRI showed reduced enhancement, and she was discharged with a prednisone taper.Ten days later, the patient returned once again to the emergency department with pain.
15. Although imaging was stable, examination revealed visual acuity of no light perception OD and new-onset right-sided third, fourth, and sixth cranial neuropathies.

12. During the following weeks, the thoracostomy tube output decreased, the tube was removed, and the patient was discharged home.

Patient_Profile:
1. A previously healthy woman in her 50s presented with complaints of increasing forgetfulness, fatigue, and depressed mood after dealing with the deaths of several close relatives.
2. She was diagnosed with depression and began treatment with antidepressant medication.
3. After 8 months, she had worsening complaints.
4. At that time, a family member reported that her memory problems had progressed.
5. She was no longer able to find misplaced objects, remember appointments, or handle financial affairs.
6. She was often subdued, her mood depressed, and her sleeping time increased.
7. Clinical examination at that time revealed a flattened affect and a 22 of 30 Mini-Mental State Examination score.
8. Findings were otherwise normal, and there were no focal neurologic deficits.
9. Basic laboratory workup results were unremarkable.
10. She was referred to a neurologist, who ordered contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain.
11. The MRI (Figure) revealed extensive ill-defined areas of FLAIR (fluid-attenuated inversion recovery) and T2 signal abnormalities with additional enhancing nodular foci located within deep white matter structures, the basal ganglia, the caudate, the pons, and the midbrain.
12. Also identified was enhancement of the interpeduncular cistern and cerebral peduncles, suggestive of leptomeningeal involvement.
13. Magnetic resonance images (MRIs) of the head obtained 8 months after patient’s first clinical visit.
14. A, Axial T2-weighted MRI of the head at the level of the lateral ventricles demonstrates extensive ill-defined areas of increasing signal with only minimal associated mass effect involving the frontal lobe white matter, greater on the left than on the right.
15. B, Contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI at the same level demonstrates abnormal patchy enhancement of the head of the left caudate nucleus and the deep anterior left frontal lobe white matter.
16. Neoplasms such as multicentric glioma, glioblastoma multiforme, and metastases

3. A clinically significant cardiac history precluded the option of surgery.

7. Approximately 5 months after treatment, he awakened with abrupt onset of severe right shoulder pain.
8. The pain was sharp, constant, and localized to his right scapula and ultimately progressed to the point of radiating down the extensor surface of his arm ending at his elbow.
9. He denied paresthesias, weakness, or any inciting events that could have led to its onset.
10. His primary care physician obtained a CT scan, followed 2 days later by a magnetic resonance image (MRI) of his right shoulder (Figure 1).

Patient_Profile:
1. A man in his late 20s presented with mildly itchy, erythematous plaques of 3 months’ duration on both legs.  
2. The lesions started to appear on the left pretibial region as small papules, which gradually increased in size and coalesced to form bigger plaques.  
3. No history of local trauma, prolonged standing, and occupational exposure to mineral dust or recent drug intake was recollected.  
4. He was not diabetic.  
5. On examination, large, ill-defined, erythematous plaques were present on the pretibial areas extending onto the lateral aspect of both legs.  
6. The plaques were surmounted by multiple, discrete atrophic scars.  
7. The periphery of the plaques showed increased vascularity in the form of telangiectasias and venous prominences, along with atrophy of the overlying skin (Figure, A).  
8. There were no lesions elsewhere on the body.  
9. A skin biopsy sample was obtained from the plaque and sent for histopathological examination (Figure, B and C).A, Clinical photograph on presentation showing ill-defined, erythematous plaques surmounted by multiple atrophic scars.  
10. The periphery of the plaques shows telangiectasia.  
11. Some areas show venous prominence.  
12. B, Skin biopsy showing unremarkable epidermis and multiple epithelioid cell granulomas in the entire dermis.  
13. C, Compact, noncaseating, epithelioid cell granulomas with multiple Langhans giant cells.  
14. D, Photograph after 6 weeks of treatment showing considerable decrease in erythema and induration.

3. Review of systems was negative for fevers, night sweats, weight loss, headache, vision changes, respiratory distress, or arthralgias.
4. On the left nasal dorsum and medial cheek, there was a 3 × 4 cm violaceous plaque with focal purulent drainage.
5. Within several weeks, the lesion rapidly expanded into a vegetative, freely draining plaque covering the cheeks and glabella and approaching the medial canthi (Figure, B).
6. Computed tomography revealed findings consistent with abscess that did not involve the orbits, sinuses, or bone.
7. Chest radiography results were unremarkable.
8. Punch biopsy specimens were obtained for histopathological analysis and tissue cultures (Figure, C).
9. Tissue culture results at 2 weeks remained negative, and a QuantiFERON-TB Gold test result was negative.A, Violaceous plaque on the nose and left cheek.
10. B, Rapid progression of the lesion involved the cheeks and glabella, with substantially worsening drainage at 6-week follow-up.
11. C, Punch biopsy of lesion showing suppurative and granulomatous dermatitis (hematoxylin-eosin).
12. D, Posttreatment, there was improvement of the lesion from initial presentation, but substantial residual facial scarring remained.

1. A middle-aged man sought treatment for a painful nonhealing foot ulcer of 1-year duration.
2. The lesion had started on the left foot as a painful blister that eventually ruptured to form an ulcer, which subsequently progressed.
3. During this time, multiple hypopigmented asymptomatic lesions appeared on his face and scalp.
4. A diagnosis of multibacillary leprosy was considered previously in another health care facility for which multidrug therapy with rifampicin, 600 mg/mo, dapsone, 100 mg/d, and clofazimine, 50 mg/d, was administered for 6 months.
5. There was no appreciable clinical improvement.
6. On physical examination, an 8 × 6-cm ulcer was noted on the lateral aspect of the dorsum of the left foot (Figure, A).
7. The ulcer was well defined with regular margins, and the floor was covered by a yellowish slough.
8. Perilesional tenderness and pitting edema were observed.
9. Multiple ill-defined, hypopigmented patches of various sizes were present on the scalp and face (Figure, B).
10. Lesional appendages and sensations were preserved.
11. Inguinal lymph nodes on both sides were enlarged, nontender, and movable.
12. Peripheral nerve trunks were not thickened, and peripheral arteries could be easily palpated.
13. Skin punch biopsy specimens were obtained from the ulcer (Figure, C and D) and a hypopigmented facial lesion.A, Nonhealing ulcer.
14. B, Ill-defined hypopigmented macules on the left side of the face.
15. Lesional skin appendages are preserved.
16. C, Histologic analysis showing acute ulceration of the epidermis with granulation tissue and infiltrating neutrophils and macrophages (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×100).
17. D, Histologic analysis showing intracellular and extracellular inclusion bodies (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×1000).

10. C, Higher magnification highlights eosinophilic material surrounding small cocci.
11. D, Gram staining of the biopsy supported the diagnosis.

1. An 8-year-old girl was referred to the vitreoretinal service for evaluation of bilateral macular lesions noted by her pediatric ophthalmologist.

5. The patient was performing well in school.  
6. On examination, her best-corrected visual acuity was 20/40 OD and 20/40 OS, which was stable from previous visits.  
7. Her pupils were round and reactive.  
8. There was a residual intermittent exotropia of 4 prism diopters bilaterally.  
9. Findings on slitlamp examination of the anterior segment were unremarkable.  
10. A single, 1-cm, oval, lightly pigmented macule with irregular borders was noted on her right upper arm.  
11. Dilated fundus examination revealed eccentric, yellow-clear, preretinal lesions in the maculas of both eyes.  
12. Optical coherence tomography revealed hyperreflective areas on the surface of the macula with a spiculated appearance, projecting anteriorly into the vitreous.  
13. There was an increase in retinal thickness and loss of the foveal contour in both eyes (Figure).  
14. Optical coherence tomography of the right eye (A) showing an atypical epiretinal membrane with anterior projection into the vitreous and hazy borders and the left eye (B) showing a similar epiretinal membrane with mild anterior projection and hazy borders.  
15. Obtain a family medical history and genetic testing Recommend pars plana vitrectomy with epiretinal membrane peel

13. No cyst, exudate, or hemorrhage was detected in the macula.

Patient_Profile:
1. A patient in their mid-30s with a medical history of deceased donor kidney transplant, cytomegalovirus (CMV) colitis, and CMV viremia with documented resistance to foscarnet and ganciclovir (UL97 and UL54 gene mutations) presented with new-onset floaters in both eyes.
2. The patient was taking systemic immunosuppression but recently stopped taking maribavir because of concerns about resistance and was transitioned to cidofovir and CMV immune globulin.
3. On clinical examination, the visual acuity measured 20/25 OD and 20/20 OS.
4. Motility, visual fields, and anterior segment examination were normal.
5. Dilated fundus examination revealed tortuous vasculature, multiple cotton wool spots along the arcades and periphery, and granular, hypopigmented retinal lesions without hemorrhage in the macula and temporal periphery in both eyes (Figure 1A).
6. Optical coherence tomography showed localized areas of full-thickness retinitis (Figure 1B).
7. CMV titers indicated viremia at 2.24 million IU/mL.
8. Despite the patient’s documented UL97 and UL54 mutations, a series of 5 biweekly intravitreal injections of foscarnet and ganciclovir were performed given their vision-threatening lesions.
9. Retinal pathology failed to improve, and the patient eventually refused additional intravitreal therapy because of pain and transiently decreased vision after each injection.Ultra-widefield fundus photograph and optical coherence tomography of a necrotic retinal lesion in the right eye demonstrating (A) multiple cotton wool spots along the arcades with retinal lesions in the temporal periphery (arrowheads) and (B) a cross-section through a temporal lesion along the superior arcade showing full thickness retinitis (arrow).

1. A 24-year-old South Asian man presented with acute-onset pain and decreased vision in his left eye.

10. Because of a concern for possible trabeculitis, he also started treatment with topical prednisolone acetate 4 times daily and oral valacyclovir hydrochloride.

5. He did not take medications, and he drank socially.

12. A computed tomography scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no malignancy.  
13. Results from cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) testing were normal without oligoclonal bands and a normal level of protein 14-3-3.  
14. He had no paraneoplastic antibodies in his serum or CSF.  
15. Results from electroencephalogram (EEG) were normal.  
16. One month later, his condition progressed; he required a wheelchair, declined cognitively, and developed personality changes.  
17. Neurological examination showed slurred speech, worsened cerebellar ataxia, and impaired postural reflex without myoclonus/asterixis.  
18. He developed seizures and was admitted to a hospital.  
19. His mental status continued to progressively decline, and he became completely mute; he could only open his eyes and follow commands to protrude his tongue but was unable to move his eyes or any limbs.

2. The patient was nonverbal at baseline and exhibited restrictive and repetitive behaviors.  
3. His diet consisted exclusively of cookies, apples, potato chips, and Gatorade.  
4. His mother noticed him frequently rubbing his eyes for several weeks, which she initially attributed to new-onset allergies.  
5. She did not describe any reduction in visual function or ability to perform low-luminance tasks.  
6. The patient was admitted and ophthalmology was consulted.  
7. He required an examination under sedation.  
8. His visual acuity could not be determined.  
9. There was no relative afferent pupillary defect in either eye.  
10. The eyelids were mildly erythematous with bilateral eyelash hypertrichosis.  
11. The conjunctiva and cornea appeared dry and leathery bilaterally.  
12. The right cornea was diffusely hazy with a 3-mm paracentral epithelial defect with 60% stromal thinning and a 1-mm infiltrate.  
13. There was a small crescentic fibrin deposit nasally in the right anterior chamber.  
14. The left cornea was diffusely hazy with a 1-mm epithelial defect without stromal thinning (Figure).  
15. Dilated examination showed bilateral grade 3 optic nerve head edema and otherwise normal retinal findings.  
16. Fortified vancomycin eye drops, 25 mg/mL, and tobramycin eye drops, 15 mg/mL, were initiated.  
17. Results of magnetic resonance imaging of the brain were normal.  
18. Photographs of the right (A) and left (B) eyes reveal a dry and lusterless appearance of the conjunctivae and corneas of both eyes.  
19. There were bilateral corneal epithelial defects with 60% stromal thinning in the right eye (arrowhead).

1. A woman in her 60s presented with a 1-month history of painless, blurred vision in the left eye.

4. Anterior segment examination results showed a relatively shallow anterior chamber in the left eye.
5. Results of a dilated fundus examination showed a choroidal detachment in the left eye extending circumferentially from the 2-o’clock to the 5-o’clock position and extending posteriorly up to 3 to 4 disc diameters temporal to the macula (Figure, A).

8. B, Anterior segment spectral domain optical coherence tomography of the left eye showing the narrow angle from suprachoroidal effusion.
9. Results of fundus fluorescein angiography of the left eye showed hypofluorescence corresponding to vitreous hemorrhage.
10. Tortuosity of the temporal vessels was prominent, with diffuse peripheral vascular leakage temporally.
11. Choroidal folds were observed 3 disc diameters temporal to the macula, extending to the periphery.
12. Peripheral capillary nonperfusion, vascular reorganization, neovascularization, and choroidal detachment were noted.
13. Anterior segment spectral domain optical coherence tomographic results showed a shallow anterior chamber and 360° narrow angles in the left eye (Figure, B).
14. Results of B-scan ultrasonography confirmed choroidal detachment in the left eye and revealed a small area of suprachoroidal effusion in the right eye in the superotemporal periphery.

11. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody testing revealed elevated proteinase 3 antibody level.
12. In the setting of anemia, infectious-disease consultants raised concern for babesiosis.
13. Peripheral blood smear and polymerase chain reaction were performed; empirical therapy of azithromycin, 500 mg daily, plus atovaquone, 750 mg twice daily, was initiated.

Patient_Profile:
1. An otherwise healthy woman in her 30s presented to an outside health care professional with a 2-day history of floaters in her left eye.
2. She denied additional ocular symptoms and reported no relevant medical, ocular, or family history; medication use; or allergies.
3. The findings of a review of systems were unremarkable.
4. A workup for posterior uveitis was initiated, and the patient began therapy with oral antiviral and oral corticosteroid medications.
5. One week later, her symptoms had worsened, and she was referred for consultation.
6. Best-corrected visual acuity was 20/15 OD and 20/60 OS.
7. Intraocular pressures, extraocular movements, visual fields by confrontation, and pupil responses were normal.
8. Anterior segment examination and dilated fundus examination of the right eye had normal findings.
9. However, the left eye had 3+ anterior chamber cell and 1+ flare, nongranulomatous keratic precipitates, and a clear lens.
10. The dilated fundus examination revealed 2+ vitritis, a hyperemic disc with blurred margins, macular striae with a blunted foveal reflex, and vascular sheathing with segmental periarteriolar inflammatory plaques in multiple quadrants.
11. The peripheral retina had well-demarcated peripheral retinal whitening with scalloped margins and intraretinal hemorrhages in all quadrants (Figure 1A and B).
12. Four days later, repeat fundus photography showed that the peripheral lesions had coalesced into larger circumferential necrotic regions (Figure 1C).
13. A, Color fundus photography montage of the left eye shows hyperemic disc with blurred margins, vascular sheathing, and peripheral retinal whitening.
14. B, Magnified image of the temporal retina shows well-demarcated infiltrates with scalloped margins and adjacent intraretinal hemorrhages.
15. C, Montage from 4 days later shows convergence of necrotic lesions in a circumferential pattern around the equator with confluence in the anterior periphery.
16. Fresh laser barricade spots are seen at the posterior margin of the areas of necrosis.

12. A bilateral ocular ultrasonography showed normal results except for vitreous opacity.
13. The patient weighed 37.0 kg and was 155 cm tall.
14. Her blood pressure was 113/70 mm Hg.
15. Mild anemia (hemoglobin level 10.5 g/dL vs a normal range of 11.0-15.0 g/dL [to convert to grams per liter, multiply by 10]) was found in routine blood test results.
16. Liver and renal functions were normal according to serum test results.
17. The results of an electronic cardiogram were negative.
18. Mosaic 9-field 50° fundus photography showed a uniform, glassy, woollike appearance of the vitreous in the right eye (A) and peripheral vitreous opacity in the left after pars plana virectomy (B).

1. On the day of giving birth via a normal vaginal delivery, a healthy woman in her 20s developed painful swelling on her right thigh, at the site of a methergine injection administered 1 day prior.
2. Despite 3 days of treatment with an oral antibiotic (cefalexin), her thigh pain and swelling did not improve, and she was readmitted to the hospital and intravenous clindamycin was started.
3. Wound cultures and blood cultures obtained during incision and drainage performed on hospital day 1 were negative for bacterial, mycobacterial, and fungal organisms.
4. The following day, her temperature was 39.4 °C (102.9 °F), blood pressure was 86/42 mm Hg, and heart rate was 131/min.
5. She was transferred to the intensive care unit for presumed septic shock, and her antibiotics were changed to vancomycin and meropenem.
6. Surgical debridement of the right thigh was performed on hospital day 3.
7. On hospital day 4, a new purple dusky border developed along the wound edge, and the patent underwent a second surgical debridement.
8. After debridement on hospital day 5, her temperature was 39.8 °C (103.6 °F), and she required vasopressor infusion with norepinephrine for shock.
9. Her right thigh had a deep 9 × 8–cm ulcer with a dusky violaceous border extending 2 to 5 cm from the wound edge (Figure, left), with many 1- to 2-mm pustules (not visible in Figure).
10. Laboratory testing showed a white blood cell count of 30 000/μL (88% neutrophils); lactate level, 77.5 mg/dL (8.6 mmol/L); and procalcitonin level, 16.1 ng/mL (reference, <0.1 ng/mL).
11. Histologic examination of the tissue obtained during the second surgical debridement revealed ulceration with extensive neutrophilic inflammation (Figure, right).
12. Stains for microorganisms, and tissue and blood cultures, remained negative.
13. Left, Patient’s right thigh showing characteristic violaceous border surrounding the surgical wound edge after multiple debridements.
14. Right, Histopathologic examination of excised tissue showing dense dermal neutrophilic infiltration (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×400).
